clue.text: Something for a religious arse steeped in drink to heave

parts.note: to sup is to drink, opened around PEW
a church bench for a churchgoer to sit on

explanation.surface: A drunken churchgoer about to be sick.
explanation.walkthrough: The religious arse is a churchgoer's backside, and a pew is what it sits on. Heave here is to retch.
explanation.definitionFit: Heave is a plain synonym in its sense of retching, and spew up is the coarse phrasal verb for being sick.

clue.text: Satisfy yourself young Mister Harry is to be heard

indicators.note: the pieces are spoken, not spelt

parts.note: Master is the title for a young boy; to bait is to harry

explanation.surface: A command to please yourself, then a boy called Harry wanting to be listened to.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Master' is the old-fashioned title for a boy, the young Mister; harry is a verb here, to harass, which is to bait.
explanation.definitionFit: A euphemism: satisfying yourself stands for sexual self-pleasure, the plain sense of the answer.

clue.text: Labour starts from here — true bastard American

indicators.note: a corrupted form, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: anagram fodder
US = American

explanation.surface: A political jibe about where the Labour Party begins, calling someone an American bastard.
explanation.walkthrough: Labour is childbirth, not the political party: contractions start in the uterus.
explanation.definitionFit: The uterus is the womb, where the labour of childbirth begins.

clue.text: (& 25dn.) Miliband, ultimately hollow, is packaged by whippersnapper as a big star

indicators.note: the inner letters are wrapped, packaged, inside the whippersnapper

parts.note: a brat is a cheeky young whippersnapper

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of Miliband is taken

parts.note: a pit is a hollow in the ground

explanation.surface: A jibe that Ed Miliband is empty at the core, wrapped up by a youngster dressed as a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: D (end of Miliband) and PIT go inside BRAT, giving BRAD PITT across the two lights.
explanation.definitionFit: Brad Pitt is a Hollywood actor, one of the biggest film stars of his generation.

clue.text: On your back, scrubbing tip of todger? That should help with semen production

definitions.text: That should help with semen production

indicators.note: a letter is scrubbed out of the word

parts.note: prostrate = lying flat; the R is removed, though the clue's 'tip of todger' would give T

explanation.surface: Someone lying back and cleaning the end of their penis.
explanation.walkthrough: PROSTRATE and PROSTATE are often confused. The parse only works by removing R, while 'tip of todger' points to T, so the clue appears to contain a slip. A todger is British slang for a penis.
explanation.definitionFit: The prostate gland produces fluid that forms part of semen.

clue.text: (& 24dn.) You'll be in grave trouble being so straight — mate indiscriminately!

definitions.text: You'll be in grave trouble being so

parts.note: dead means directly or exactly, as in dead straight or dead ahead

indicators.note: the letters of mate are taken in no particular order, mixed up

explanation.surface: A warning that playing it straight, or mating with anyone, lands you in a grave.
explanation.walkthrough: DEAD is followed by MEAT, the letters of MATE rearranged; 'grave' doubles as the burial plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone called dead meat is doomed and in serious trouble, the slang threat of being finished.

clue.text: Balls gets not much applause, having coarse mouth

parts.note: a single clap is scant applause
trap is coarse slang for mouth, as in 'shut your trap'

explanation.surface: Someone called Balls gets a feeble response for being foul-mouthed.
explanation.walkthrough: Balls looks like Ed Balls, the Labour politician, but it is the slang for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Balls is slang for nonsense, which is claptrap.

clue.text: Players pissed round toilet's entrance — it took some pluck in the old days

definitions.text: it took some pluck in the old days

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder, arranged around the T

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

parts.note: first letter of toilet

explanation.surface: A band of drunken musicians gathered round the lavatory door.
explanation.walkthrough: The pluck is literal: a psaltery was a medieval stringed instrument played by plucking, so the definition is a cryptic hint rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A psaltery is an old plucked stringed instrument, so it took some plucking in the old days.

clue.text: Tory no. 2 teamed with pisspoor, energy-lacking leader — nightmare!

indicators.note: take the second letter of Tory
a badly done version of the word, so its letters are jumbled
remove E, the symbol for energy

parts.note: second letter of Tory
LEADER minus one E (energy) leaves LADER, rearranged to RDEAL

explanation.surface: A jibe that a Tory deputy paired with a feeble, listless leader would be a nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Teamed with' only puts the two pieces side by side. The anagram works on LADER, the five letters left once one E is gone.
explanation.definitionFit: Figurative use: a nightmare is any dreadful experience, and an ordeal is the painful trial one has to live through.

clue.text: About Rev. Blair's capital cash dispenser: one inside's reported with no change

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the word Rev is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written: the clerical title

indicators.note: the capital, the initial letter, of Blair's is taken
the one goes inside, the 's being is

parts.note: ATM, automated teller machine, is a cash dispenser
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A satirical jab at the Reverend Tony Blair's cash machine, with someone on the inside reporting everything word for word.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' turns REV into VER, B is Blair's capital letter, and I goes inside ATM to make ATIM.
explanation.definitionFit: Verbatim means word for word, so a speech reported verbatim is repeated exactly as given.

clue.text: John leaves the battle site — wet!

parts.note: Waterloo, where Napoleon was defeated in 1815
john is slang for a toilet, as is loo; removed from WATERLOO

explanation.surface: Someone named John walking off a famous battlefield in the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: John looks like a man's name but is the slang word for a toilet. A loo is the British word for a toilet.
explanation.definitionFit: Wet can be a noun for rain or liquid, which is water.

clue.text: Put a spin on Ed's super balls-up, following Miliband's last one

indicators.note: the scrambled letters follow the letter from Miliband, so that letter leads
last one points to the final letter of Miliband's name

parts.note: the surname Miliband, the 's tying it to the letter taken

indicators.note: a balls-up is a mess, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Political spin on Ed Miliband's big blunder, coming after his previous one.
explanation.walkthrough: D, the last of Miliband, comes first; then EDS and SUPER are jumbled into RESSEDUP.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress something up is to present it more attractively than it deserves, which is what spin does.

clue.text: Pervy as a prole on getting end away producing UV protection device

indicators.note: pervy, a twisted kind of thing, signals that the letters are bent into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: the word loses its last letter; also Private Eye's slang for sex

parts.note: prole is a working-class person; minus its end it becomes PROL

explanation.surface: A sleazy working-class man is caught having sex, in Private Eye's crude style.
explanation.walkthrough: PROLE without its last letter is PROL; mixed with AS and A, the letters give PARASOL.
explanation.definitionFit: A parasol is a light umbrella carried to shade the user from the sun's ultraviolet rays.

clue.text: Monument? Come down to earth, Thatcher!

parts.note: to land is to come down to the ground
Mark Thatcher, son of Margaret Thatcher

explanation.surface: A call for Mrs Thatcher to be realistic about her own monument.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher looks like Margaret, the former prime minister, but it is her son Mark. The question mark makes the definition tentative.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a monument is one kind of landmark, a conspicuous structure people navigate by or visit.

clue.text: Blair broadcast dropped by summer — which peer takes the piss out of

definitions.text: which peer takes the piss out of

indicators.note: the word for broadcast is dropped from the former prime minister's name

parts.note: to air is to broadcast
one who sums, or adds up, is an adder

explanation.surface: A mocking peer drops Tony Blair's broadcasts for the summer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'summer' is not the season but one who sums. 'peer' plays on pee-er, someone who urinates.
explanation.definitionFit: This organ stores urine, so anyone urinating empties it, literally taking the piss out of it.

clue.text: Howe, leader-wise in awful dread yet, departs (the "wet" having been got rid of)

indicators.note: in the manner of a leader, meaning only the letter at the front of Howe
a mess, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: first letter of Howe
anagram fodder
d = departs, as on timetables

explanation.surface: Geoffrey Howe fearfully quitting, the 'wets' having been purged.
explanation.walkthrough: Geoffrey Howe was a Thatcher-era minister, and the 'wets' were her moderate Tory opponents. Here the wet is simply water, removed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dehydrated has had its water, the wet, removed.

clue.text: Very speedy article by Nick leads to arse-kicking

parts.note: as in 'a cracking pace'
the definite article
to nick and to whip are both British slang for steal

explanation.surface: A fast piece of writing by someone named Nick prompting a good kicking.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick looks like a name but is British slang for steal, as is whip. Cracking the whip is making people work hard, as a verb-phrase noun matching arse-kicking.
explanation.definitionFit: Cracking the whip means imposing strict discipline, which is what arse-kicking means figuratively.

clue.text: Bring some culture to Channel Islands Elvis impersonator, initially crap

parts.note: CI is the abbreviation for the Channel Islands, such as Jersey and Guernsey

indicators.note: crap here means poor or rubbish, so the letters are a botched arrangement
initially means the first letter of impersonator is taken

explanation.surface: Trying to educate a terrible Elvis tribute act on Jersey or Guernsey.
explanation.walkthrough: After CI, the letters of ELVIS plus I (impersonator's first letter) are rearranged as VILISE.
explanation.definitionFit: To civilise people is to bring them refinement and education, improving their manners and culture.

clue.text: Charity gives Brand head

parts.note: a brand is a kind or sort
a ness is a headland, as in Loch Ness

explanation.surface: A charity awarding Russell Brand a leading role.
explanation.walkthrough: Brand looks like the comedian Russell Brand, but it means a kind. Ness is a headland in place names.
explanation.definitionFit: Charity in its older sense of love for others is a plain synonym, not the donation-collecting organisation the surface suggests.

clue.text: Country's massive performer of hot blow job consumed by energy

parts.note: vim = energy, split to hold ETNA

parts.words: massive performer of hot blow job
parts.note: Etna, a huge volcano whose job is to blow out hot lava

explanation.surface: A smutty tale of a large performer and a sex act swallowed up by energy.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'blow job' is a volcano's eruption, not a sex act: Etna in Sicily is a massive volcano. The 's after Country is 'has', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Vietnam is a country in South-East Asia.

clue.text: Disposer of bull, thanks to party getting into arm twisting

indicators.note: thanks and party get into the twisted arm
twisting arm rearranges its letters

parts.note: ta is British informal for thanks
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Thanks to a party, someone resorts to arm-twisting to get rid of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bull' looks like slang for nonsense but means the animal in the ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A matador is the bullfighter who kills the bull at the climax of the fight.

clue.text: A certain nursery rhyme miss's mound? Express disapproval and eff off inside

definitions.text: A certain nursery rhyme miss's mound

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go inside the disapproving word

parts.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval

indicators.note: off means gone bad or wrong, so the letters of eff are disordered

explanation.surface: Annoyance at Little Miss Muffet's seat, telling someone to clear off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' rearranges EFF into FFE, which goes inside TUT. Little Miss Muffet, in the nursery rhyme, 'sat on a tuffet'.
explanation.definitionFit: A tuffet is a low seat or grassy hillock, the one Miss Muffet sat on in the nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Related to the place turning out shit claret (canned)

definitions.text: Related to the place turning out shit

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A vineyard producing a terrible red wine, drunk anyway.
explanation.walkthrough: Canned is British slang for drunk. The place turning out shit reads like a bad winery but is the rectum.
explanation.definitionFit: Rectal means relating to the rectum, where faeces leave the body.

clue.text: Sweet old men, screwed by pro, having a turn

indicators.note: twisted out of shape, so the letters are rearranged
the letters are turned about

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder, a pro being a prostitute in the surface

explanation.surface: Nice old gentlemen, visited by a prostitute, each taking a turn.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweet looks like an adjective describing the old men, but it is a noun: a sweet is British for a piece of candy.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: sweet is the British word for any candy, and a lemon drop is one type of it.

clue.text: see 6dn.
see 4dn.
The old Frenchman's ready to kick butt off dictator

indicators.note: the butt, or tail end, of the word is removed

parts.note: Franco, dictator of Spain; losing his final O

explanation.surface: A plea to an old Frenchman that he is ready to boot out a tyrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is British slang for cash, not a word meaning prepared. The franc was France's currency before the euro, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: The franc was the French person's money, their ready cash, before the euro replaced it.

clue.text: Being skimpy, what boxers might do — slacken elastic tops

parts.note: boxers spar in practice

indicators.note: the top, or first, letters of slacken and elastic

parts.note: first letters of slacken and elastic

explanation.surface: Men's boxer shorts being skimpy, their elastic waistbands slackening.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures boxer shorts with tired elastic; the boxers are fighters instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Being skimpy means being scant or thin, which is sparse.

clue.text: Two Tory leaders EEC trashed are ruined, and similar things

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked, so these letters are thrown into a new order
the leaders of words are their opening letters

parts.note: its first letter is T
its first letter is T
taken as written: the European Economic Community

indicators.note: ruined says these letters are spoilt and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tory leaders wreck the European Economic Community and are themselves undone.
explanation.walkthrough: Two T's from 'Two Tory' join EEC, and 'trashed' rearranges those letters into ETCET; 'ruined' turns ARE into ERA.
explanation.definitionFit: Et cetera is Latin for 'and the rest', used to stand for further items of the same kind.
